newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to offer upbeat economic and EMU outlook.
newsitem.headline: EU to offer upbeat economic and EMU outlook.

text.p: Stronger economic growth and a glowing assessment of the progress governments are making towards qualifying for a common currency are expected from the European Commission on Wednesday.
According to some reports, as many as 13 of the bloc's 15 members may be deemed to be on track to adopt the euro, as the new currency will be known, on January 1, 1999.

In its twice-yearly ritual, the EU's executive is expected to say that economic growth has recovered after stumbling earlier this year, powered by a stronger recovery in Germany, the Union's economic powerhouse.
In May, the Commission downgraded its overall growth forecast for the 15-nation bloc to 1.5 percent in 1996 after economic activity slowed unexpectedly towards the end of 1995.
Commission and monetary sources now expect that the 1996 growth figure to be released with the forecasts will be higher. They will also offer an improved growth assessment for 1997.

The rosier outlook is in line with the prediction last week by six leading German economic institutes that Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) will grow 1.5 percent this year. The Commission's spring forecast was based on German growth of just 0.5 percent.

More controversially, the exercise is also expected to show that a large majority of the 15 member states will meet the EU's key budget deficit target of three percent of GDP in 1997, the year on which countries' ability to join its planned single currency in 1999 will be judged.

On Tuesday a Lisbon-based newspaper, citing official figures, said the Commission would show 13 governments meeting the Maastricht's deficit criteria, with only Italy and Greece not qualifying. In May, the Commission said only seven had their deficits in line with the criteria.
Although keeping the details close to his chest, EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy has said he expects the figures to show more countries heading for qualification.

But whether such a snapshot of budgetary improvement is an accurate reflection of durable convergence is currently under debate, with countries such as Germany voicing concern over one-off measures taken to meet the Maastricht criteria.
The most controversial has been the go-ahead given to France to use 37.5 billion francs ($7.3 billion) transferred from state telephone company France Telecom to reduce its huge budget deficit.
The decision opens the way for further desperate, last-minute efforts, using what some critics call creative accounting methods, to meet the targets for monetary union.
At a minimum, the favourable verdict for France will prompt others to call for the same treatment.

On Monday, Spain's Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told journalists that the country's economic health must be judged by the same yardstick as France's when the selection is made for joining the single currency.
The primary worry of a single currency formed with too many countries in 1999 is that it will be perceived as relatively weak by investors.

Overall the Commission's forecasting exercise is increasingly viewed with cynicism by financial markets, aware of the political pressure the body is under to put the best light on the EMU convergence process.
"It's not an independent analyst looking at Europe from the moon," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris.
As such there is little expectation that Wednesday's economic review will surprise investors or prompt much of a market reaction.
